items.title: The 'inert' gases are not entirely inert
items.claim: Argon, krypton, xenon and radon all form chemical compounds. XeF2, XeF4 and XeF6 are stable solids that can be bought from chemical suppliers. The textbook claim that noble gases 'don't react' is a simplification.
items.prompt: Why can xenon — but not helium or neon — form compounds?

options.text: Xenon has a different number of valence electrons

Xenon's outer electrons are far from the nucleus and weakly held (low ionisation energy, 1170 kJ/mol); the strongest oxidisers like PtF6 and F2 can strip or share them. Helium and neon hold their electrons too tightly
Xenon contains a hidden valence electron

items.reveal:
Until 1962, every chemistry textbook said noble gases were entirely unreactive. Neil Bartlett at the University of British Columbia noticed that O2's ionisation energy (1175 kJ/mol) is essentially the same as xenon's (1170 kJ/mol). He had just shown PtF6 could oxidise O2. So PtF6 should be able to oxidise xenon. He tried it. XePtF6 formed instantly.

XeF2 is now made by simply mixing Xe and F2 in sunlight. XeF4 forms colourless crystals. XeO3 is a powerful explosive. Krypton compounds (KrF2) exist at low temperature. Even argon was forced to form HArF in 2000.

Helium and neon, the lightest noble gases, have ionisation energies around 2080 and 2370 kJ/mol — too high to be broken even by the strongest oxidisers in normal conditions.
items.why: 'Inert' is a useful summary, not a law of nature. Strong enough chemistry breaks even the rule of full octets.

items.title: Chromatography separates by retention, not by size
items.claim: Drop coloured ink on filter paper and dip the edge in water. The colours separate into bands. The colours that travel furthest aren't the smallest — they spend more time in the moving solvent and less time stuck to the paper.

options.text: Each component has its own equilibrium between the mobile phase (solvent) and the stationary phase (paper or silica); components that prefer the solvent travel fast, those that prefer the stationary phase travel slowly

items.reveal:
Rf = distance travelled by component / distance travelled by solvent front. Always between 0 and 1, characteristic of a molecule for a given solvent and stationary phase.

A polar molecule with many H-bond donors sticks to polar silica or paper and has Rf close to 0. A non-polar molecule prefers a non-polar solvent and has Rf close to 1.

This principle scales up to billion-dollar industrial chromatography for drug purification — same physics, bigger columns and more elaborate detectors. HPLC, GC, ion exchange and size exclusion all derive from the same competitive-equilibrium concept.
items.why: Chromatography is taught as 'big vs small'. The mechanism is competitive equilibrium between two phases — and that's what makes it so versatile.

items.title: An 18-year-old's failed antimalarial attempt founded the synthetic dye industry
items.claim: In 1856 William Henry Perkin, an 18-year-old chemistry student in London, was trying to synthesise the antimalarial quinine from coal tar. He failed. The black sludge he produced, when washed with alcohol, gave a brilliant purple solution. He had made mauveine — the first synthetic dye.
items.prompt: Why did Perkin's mauve change the world?

options.text: It launched the synthetic organic dye industry, which became the seedbed of pharmaceutical chemistry, plastics, photography and modern industrial chemistry — particularly in Germany

items.reveal:
Perkin was working in his home laboratory during the Easter holiday. The bench was a board across the bathtub. He oxidised aniline (from coal tar) with potassium dichromate and got a tarry mess. Cleaning the flask with alcohol, he noticed an intense purple solution.

He filed a patent (despite being a minor), set up a factory at age 19 with his father and brother, and made a fortune. Queen Victoria wore mauve to her daughter's wedding in 1858. The colour exploded across European fashion.

Germany rapidly built on the industry. By 1900 BASF, Hoechst, Bayer and Agfa dominated synthetic chemistry and were turning out hundreds of new dyes. Aspirin (Bayer, 1899) and Salvarsan (Ehrlich, 1909) came out of the same dye-research tradition.

Perkin retired wealthy at 36 to do pure research.
items.why: An accidental failure can found an entire industry. The dye industry seeded pharmaceutical chemistry and modern materials science.
